children: Analytics and artificial-intelligence software firm Databricks says its business in Asia is accelerating and plans to invest more in Singapore to tap regional demand.

Simon Davies, who heads the San Francisco-based company's business in Asia Pacific and Japan, said Wednesday in an interview that Databricks' business in the region more than doubled in the second quarter, making it the company's fastest growing market.

Databricks is one of Silicon Valley's most valuable startups, as the artificial intelligence boom drives demand for the company's data-analytics software. The unicorn is among a crop of companies long considered candidates for public listings.
The firm was valued at $190 billion after a fundraising round in August led by Coatue, along with Blackstone, MGX, T. Rowe Price, and Sixth Street Growth.
"We've been quite aggressive in capital markets raising funds. Part of that is to allow us to continue to invest heavily in new capabilities," Davies said.

The company plans invest more than $350 million in Singapore over the next three years to tap the region's demand, and will double its headcount in the city-state to over 500. A significant part of that investment will be in technical capabilities for engineers and tech specialists, Davies said.
The company has already invested over $1 billion in the region, he said.
"Asia-Pacific is the fastest-growing [region] and the plan is for us to continue to be the fastest-growing in the years to come," Davies said.
Databricks plans to ramp up hiring in Asia, up from the current 1,500 employees it has in the region, he added.
The company is growing rapidly, generating a revenue run rate of $7 billion, it said in August, up from $5.4 billion in February.
It recently released a new software tool, called Unity AI Gateway, that allows companies to access AI models and track their spending on the technology.
"Costs I would say is one of the most top of mind issues for all of our customers," Davies said. "The technology could be amazing, but is it going to be cost-effective?"

The company also recently launched Genie One, an agentic AI assistant that answers employees' questions and helps automate tasks, which is an area that the company is heavily investing in, Davies said.

The challenge of customers moving from prototype or pilot to production, as well as executing governance and security requirements, is a big factor fueling a lot of growth and demand for its AI agents in Asia, he said.

Databricks' earlier investors include Andreessen Horowitz, NEA, Insight Partners, Fidelity Management & Research Co. and J.P. Morgan Asset Management. Coatue, the New York-based hedge and venture fund, is a longtime investor in Databricks.

"The business scale, the growth that we're seeing will always create challenges," he said. "We're opening new offices. We've got lots of other plans across the region. Laws of physics of bricks and mortar will always mean it takes time."
